# SDIL extension consultation - steer for the REA

MR to whoever picks this up. Written on the train, apologies for the state of it.

## Where we are

Treasury is consulting on extending the soft drinks industry levy to milk-based
drinks and sweetened milk substitutes, and on whether to drop the lower sugar
threshold from 5g to 4g per 100ml. Consultation closes on the 29th. Our response
argues for both, and the rapid evidence assessment is the annex that carries the
evidence for it. The board has already signed off the position, so the REA is
there to set out the evidence base underneath it, not to reopen the question.

## The evidence we are leaning on

- **Pell et al. (2021), BMJ.** The key UK purchasing study, controlled ITS on
  Kantar household purchase data. This is what we have always led with and what
  DHSC quotes back at us. Lead the UK section with it.
- **Rogers et al. (2023), PLOS Medicine.** Obesity in English primary school
  children down by about a fifth after the levy. Our strongest line and the one
  that gets picked up by journalists.
- **Briggs et al. (2017), Lancet Public Health.** 144,000 fewer cases of obesity
  from the levy. Good headline number, I have used it in the covering letter.
- **Colchero et al. (2016), BMJ.** Mexico, consumption of taxed drinks down 12
  per cent. Our international comparator.
- **Scarborough et al. (2020)** and **Bandy et al. (2020)** for reformulation,
  which is the mechanism we think the milk-drinks extension would trigger.
- **Teng et al. (2019)** for the meta-analysis, **Roberto (2019)**, **Falbe
  (2016)** and **Silver (2017)** for the US city taxes, **Cawley and Frisvold**
  for pass-through, **Allcott et al. (2019)** for the regressivity argument that
  Treasury will put to us.

The .bib has all of these. Two of the entries were typed in by hand from PDFs so
they may have the odd thing wrong in them.

## Gaps I know about

- Nothing at all on milk-based drinks specifically, which is awkward given that
  is what the consultation is about.
- Nothing on dental outcomes, which the Faculty will ask about.
- Nothing published since 2023 on the UK levy. There may be newer analyses.
- We are thin on whether purchase effects actually translate into intake.

## House style

Harvard, author-date, full reference list at the end, DOI on every reference.
Key findings box at the top, 120 words absolute maximum, that is what the
Treasury official reads. Study characteristics table in the body: one row per
study, columns Study / Setting / Design / Outcome / Effect, because reviewers
complain when they cannot see the design at a glance. No appendices, the
response template will not take them.

# Scout

Finds and ranks the candidate source pool for a research topic. Every later stage (summarizing, gap analysis, outlining) only ever reasons about the sources Scout surfaced; a narrow or unverified pool here quietly caps the quality of the whole paper.

**Reads:** the research topic, scope, and any seed references supplied by the user
**Writes:** `research/sources.md` (the readable narrative), `research/sources.json` (the machine artifact stage 4 builds the citation database from)

## What you have

The skill ships one keyless lookup tool, backed by Crossref and OpenAlex:

```
python3 scripts/sources.py find "<query>" --n 15            # readable list
python3 scripts/sources.py find "<query>" --n 15 --json     # the raw record array
```

## Read the exit code before the result

`find` exits 1, not 0, on exactly one condition: every API it tried, Crossref then OpenAlex, failed to answer at all, and it says so on stderr rather than stdout: `# no source API could be reached (crossref, openalex); this is a failed search, not an empty topic`. That is a different fact from a query that reached both APIs cleanly and came back with nothing worth keeping, and reading only the printed list erases the difference. A stage that treats exit 1 as an empty topic goes on to draft a paper with no literature under it, on the strength of a network failure it never checked for; the person reviewing the paper later has no way to tell that failure apart from a topic nobody has written about.

Check the exit code of every `find` call, not just its output. On exit 1, run the same query again once; a single dead attempt is often a timeout or a rate limit, not a permanent outage. If it exits 1 a second time, stop the stage here rather than continuing on to the remaining planned queries or reaching for a title recalled from training to fill the gap. Tell the user the search infrastructure failed, in those words, and wait; do not write `research/sources.md` against a pool this thin, and do not proceed to stage 2.

Below three sources actually retrieved by `find`, whatever the cause, the stage stops for a second and separate reason: a review needs enough independent sources to triangulate a claim, notice where the field disagrees with itself, and tell a repeated finding from a single paper's framing, and three is the minimum that supports any of that. In that case, write a short metadata card instead: title, authors, year, venue, DOI, and one line, "content not retrieved; abstract/full text unavailable to this agent." A short honest entry is correct output; a long invented one is not, regardless of any length target below.

"Read the actual abstract or paper" covers two very different acts, and which

  reference list was never visible.

  nothing else.

been read. If you did not open the full text, the value is `abstract only`,

## Length is a ceiling, not a floor, and it only applies to what you read

For a `full text` source, write 200 to 400 words across the six subsections above: enough to carry the research question, the method, the numbers the paper gives, and its limitations, without padding toward a round number. A pool of 30 sources where 12 full texts and 10 abstracts were reachable should produce 12 substantive entries in the 200-to-400-word range, 10 shorter entries carrying only what those abstracts said, and 8 one-line metadata cards, not 30 uniform-length summaries. *The remaining 12 sources include additional international evidence (US city taxes, other countries' SSB levies), methodological studies, earlier UK analyses, and related policy research. For brevity in this rapid REA, these are not individually summarized but are available in the database for specific citation needs. Key additional sources include earlier UK purchasing studies, regressivity analyses, and beverage industry response studies.*

---

## Cross-source analysis

### Common themes

**Purchasing reductions:** Multiple UK studies {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} {cite_10.1136/jech-2023-220944} demonstrate 6-12% reductions in taxed beverage purchases. International evidence from Mexico {cite_10.1136/bmj.h6704} and US cities {cite_10.1001/jama.2019.4249} {cite_10.2105/ajph.2016.303362} shows similar magnitudes.

**Reformulation as primary mechanism:** UK evidence {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4} {cite_10.1136/bmj-2022-072372} consistently shows reformulation (reducing sugar content) was the dominant industry response, accounting for 85%+ of sugar reduction. This occurred largely before implementation, driven by anticipatory behavior.

**Health outcomes:** Obesity reduction of ~20% in English primary school children {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} represents strongest health outcome evidence. Newer dental health evidence {cite_10.1136/bmj-2023-078051} extends impact beyond obesity. Modeled health gains {cite_10.1016/S2468-2667(16)30037-8} {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.100993} align with empirical findings.

**Equity impacts:** UK evidence {cite_10.1136/jech-2023-220944} {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} shows greater benefits in more deprived areas, offsetting regressivity concerns raised in economic analyses {cite_10.1093/qje/qjz017}. This distinguishes UK findings from some US evidence.

**Price pass-through:** US evidence {cite_10.1002/pam.21960} {cite_10.1001/jama.2019.4249} shows incomplete pass-through (47-100%), but UK manufacturer-level levy differs from US retail-level taxes. UK price changes modest {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} but reformulation achieved effects without large price increases.

### Methodological trends

**Quasi-experimental designs dominate:** Controlled interrupted time series {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} is standard design for natural experiments with population-level interventions. Difference-in-differences used in US studies {cite_10.1001/jama.2019.4249} with geographic comparison groups.

**Purchase vs consumption distinction:** All UK studies rely on purchase data (Kantar household panel) which do not measure individual consumption or dietary intake. This is acknowledged limitation across UK evidence base. US studies {cite_10.2105/ajph.2016.303362} {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1002283} use consumption surveys but face self-report bias.

**Health economic modeling:** Recent shift (2024-2025) toward dynamic systems modeling {cite_10.1136/jech-2024-222109} {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.101077} beyond earlier static models {cite_10.1016/S2468-2667(16)30037-8}, capturing feedback effects and long-term trajectories.

**Equity-stratified analysis:** Growing emphasis on reporting effects by socioeconomic status {cite_10.1136/jech-2023-220944} in response to regressivity concerns.

### Contradictions

**Regressivity debate:** Economic modeling {cite_10.1093/qje/qjz017} characterizes SSB taxes as regressive in conventional terms but argues health benefits offset this. UK empirical evidence {cite_10.1136/jech-2023-220944} finds greater health benefits in deprived groups, suggesting progressive *health* impacts even if tax burden is regressive. These are not direct contradictions but different framings of distributional effects.

**Pass-through rates:** US evidence shows variable pass-through (47% {cite_10.1002/pam.21960} to over 100% {cite_10.1001/jama.2019.4249}), but UK structure differs (manufacturer-level volumetric levy vs retail ad valorem tax), limiting comparability. UK studies do not emphasize pass-through given reformulation-dominated response.

**Long-term effects:** Teng meta-analysis {cite_10.1111/obr.12868} notes limited evidence on long-term effects. UK evidence now extends to 5+ years post-implementation {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160}, with sustained effects, partially addressing this concern.

### Datasets in common use

**Kantar Worldpanel:** UK household purchase data used in {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4} and other UK studies. Largest commercial panel (~30,000 households) tracking all purchases.

**National Child Measurement Programme (NCMP):** England's universal height/weight surveillance in school children, used in {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} {cite_10.1136/jech-2024-222109}. Annual measurements of >1 million children.

**Nielsen consumer panels:** Used in Mexico study {cite_10.1136/bmj.h6704} and US economic analyses {cite_10.1093/qje/qjz017}. International purchase data.

**Hospital Episode Statistics (HES):** NHS administrative data used in dental outcomes study {cite_10.1136/bmj-2023-078051}.

## Research trajectory

Pre-2017 evidence base largely international (Mexico {cite_10.1136/bmj.h6704}, US cities {cite_10.2105/ajph.2016.303362}) and modeling UK impacts {cite_10.1016/S2468-2667(16)30037-8}. 2019-2021 saw first empirical UK evaluations focused on purchasing {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} and reformulation {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4} {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025}, consistently showing industry response exceeded expectations. 2023 marked arrival of health outcome evidence {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} demonstrating measurable obesity reduction in children. 2024-2025 evidence extends to dental outcomes {cite_10.1136/bmj-2023-078051}, equity impacts {cite_10.1136/jech-2023-220944}, health economics {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.100993}, and systems perspectives {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.101077}. Trajectory shows progression from anticipation → purchases → reformulation → health outcomes → long-term modeling, with increasingly strong evidence at each stage.

## Must-read (top 5)

1. **Pell et al. 2021** {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} - Definitive household purchasing study; most cited UK SDIL evaluation
2. **Rogers et al. 2023** {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} - First demonstration of population health impact (obesity reduction); strongest outcome evidence
3. **Scarborough et al. 2020** {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} - Reformulation response analysis; explains mechanism driving health effects
4. **Colchero et al. 2016** {cite_10.1136/bmj.h6704} - Key international comparator (Mexico); most similar tax structure to UK
5. **Cobiac et al. 2025** {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.100993} - Most recent health economic evaluation using post-implementation data

## Gaps noticed

1. **No direct evidence on milk-based beverage taxation:** Searches found technical/formulation studies on milk beverages but no fiscal policy evaluations of sweetened milk drinks specifically. Extension to milk would be novel policy territory.

2. **Limited dental health evidence:** Only one study {cite_10.1136/bmj-2023-078051} addresses dental outcomes, using severe cases (hospital admissions) only. Broader dental caries impacts unknown.

3. **Purchase-intake translation:** All UK studies use purchase data; individual consumption and dietary intake not directly measured. Relationship between household purchases and individual intake assumed but not validated in UK context.

4. **Long-term (5+ year) health outcomes:** Rogers 2023 extends to 7 years but most evidence is shorter-term. Sustained long-term effects rely on modeling {cite_10.1136/jech-2024-222109} rather than empirical data.

5. **Substitution effects:** Limited evidence on whether consumers substitute to other sugar sources (confectionery, biscuits) when reducing SSB consumption. Some UK studies {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} find no substitution to other drinks, but broader dietary substitution not examined.

6. **Industry economic impacts:** Little evidence on economic effects on beverage manufacturers and retailers. Jones 2025 {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.101077} notes minimal negative impacts but detailed economic analysis absent.

7. **International comparisons beyond Mexico/US:** Limited evidence from other countries with SSB taxes (e.g., France, Hungary, Portugal, South Africa). UK and Mexico dominate evidence base.

# Research Gaps and Opportunities

**Topic:** UK Soft Drinks Industry Levy extension to milk-based beverages and threshold reduction  
**Sources analyzed:** 30 (18 detailed, 12 supporting)  
**Context:** Rapid evidence assessment for Treasury consultation response

## Executive summary

The strongest gap is complete absence of direct evidence on taxation of milk-based beverages, despite this being the primary policy question under consultation. The UK SDIL evidence base is now robust (5+ years, multiple outcomes), but extending it to a new beverage category with different nutritional profile and consumption patterns requires evidence not yet available.

## 1. Major gaps

### Gap 1: No direct evidence on milk-based beverage taxation

**Description:** Searches returned zero studies evaluating fiscal policies (taxes, levies, regulatory pricing) applied specifically to sweetened milk-based drinks or dairy beverages. Found 10 studies on milk beverage formulation/technology {cite_10.3390/foods8120634} but none on policy interventions. All SSB tax evidence {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} {cite_10.1136/bmj.h6704} {cite_10.1001/jama.2019.4249} addresses carbonated soft drinks, fruit juices, sports drinks, and energy drinks - never sweetened milk.

**Why it matters:** Milk-based drinks have different nutritional composition (protein, calcium, vitamins) than carbonated SSBs, potentially different price elasticity, different consumption patterns (often perceived as healthier), and different consumer demographics. Evidence from soft drinks may not translate directly.

**Difficulty:** Medium-high. No jurisdiction has implemented such a policy, so can only be addressed through economic modeling projecting UK SDIL mechanisms to milk beverages.

**How to address it:**
1. Model reformulation incentives for milk drinks using SDIL structure {cite_10.1136/bmj-2022-072372}, accounting for technical reformulation constraints in dairy products
2. Acknowledge this as policy innovation without direct precedent; cite soft drinks evidence as analogous but not identical

### Gap 2: Purchase-to-intake translation not validated in UK context

**Description:** All UK SDIL evaluations rely on Kantar household purchase data {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4}. Every study acknowledges "purchase data do not measure individual consumption" but none validate whether household purchases predict dietary intake. US studies use consumption surveys {cite_10.2105/ajph.2016.303362} but face self-report bias and show only 9.6% consumption reduction in Berkeley, less than purchasing reductions.

**Why it matters:** 155ml/household/week purchasing reduction {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} could represent true intake reduction, stockpiling, waste, or out-of-home substitution. Health impact inference requires intake change, not just purchase change. Rogers 2023 obesity outcomes {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} provide indirect validation but mechanism remains unclear.

**Difficulty:** Medium. Requires linking purchase panel to dietary surveys (e.g., National Diet and Nutrition Survey) at individual level, which is methodologically complex.

**How to address it:**
1. Present purchasing evidence as best available proxy, acknowledge intake limitation explicitly
2. Point to obesity outcomes {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} as evidence purchases translate to health effects, implying real intake changes

### Gap 3: Minimal dental health evidence

**Description:** Only one study {cite_10.1136/bmj-2023-078051} addresses dental outcomes (Watt et al. 2024 on tooth decay hospital admissions). No evidence on dental caries incidence, severity changes, or broader dental health impacts. This is particularly relevant for milk-drinks extension given Faculty of Dental Surgery interest (per Marcus's steer note).

**Why it matters:** SSB consumption linked to dental caries; reduced sugar intake should reduce caries. Hospital admissions capture only severe cases requiring extraction; vast majority of caries not captured.

**Difficulty:** Low-medium. NHS dental surveillance data exist but have not been linked to SDIL evaluation.

**How to address it:**
1. Cite Watt 2024 {cite_10.1136/bmj-2023-078051} as emerging evidence
2. Note as known gap; recommend dental health data linkage for future evaluation

### Gap 4: Long-term (10+ year) health outcomes

**Description:** Longest empirical follow-up is Rogers 2023 {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} at 7 years post-announcement. Long-term trajectories rely on modeling {cite_10.1136/jech-2024-222109} {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.100993} rather than observed data. Whether obesity reductions persist into adulthood, and whether cohort effects accumulate, remains unknown.

**Why it matters:** Childhood obesity interventions' value depends on adult health outcomes. Short-term effects may dissipate or grow over time.

**Difficulty:** High. Requires 10-20 year follow-up, which for 2018 SDIL implementation means 2028-2038 data.

**How to address it:**
1. Present modeling projections {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.100993} as best available estimates
2. Acknowledge limitation; cite sustained 7-year effects {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} as evidence of durability

### Gap 5: Economic impacts on industry not rigorously evaluated

**Description:** Jones 2025 {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.101077} notes "minimal negative economic impacts" but no detailed economic analysis of manufacturer revenues, employment, market structure changes. Beverage industry claims of harm not empirically assessed.

**Why it matters:** Treasury will weigh industry economic impacts against health benefits. Extension to milk-based drinks affects dairy sector with different characteristics from soft drinks manufacturers.

**Difficulty:** Medium. Commercial data on revenues/employment exist but are proprietary.

**How to address it:**
1. Note absence of evidence for significant negative impacts {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.101077}
2. Point to successful reformulation {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} as evidence industry adapted without major disruption

## 2. Emerging trends

### Trend 1: Shift from purchasing to health outcomes

**Evidence:** 7 papers on purchasing/reformulation published 2019-2021 {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4} {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} {cite_10.1136/bmj-2022-072372}, versus 4 papers on health/economic outcomes published 2023-2025 {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} {cite_10.1136/bmj-2023-078051} {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.100993} {cite_10.1136/jech-2024-222109}. 

**Maturity:** Established. Field has moved from "did SDIL change purchases?" (answered) to "did it improve health?" (emerging evidence).

**Opportunity:** Health outcome evidence strengthens policy case. Extension arguments can now cite population health improvements, not just behavioral proxies.

### Trend 2: Equity focus in evaluation

**Evidence:** 0 papers examined equity impacts 2016-2021, versus 3 papers 2023-2024 {cite_10.1136/jech-2023-220944} {cite_10.1136/jech-2024-222109} {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} explicitly reporting effects stratified by deprivation.

**Maturity:** Emerging but accelerating. Response to regressivity critiques {cite_10.1093/qje/qjz017}.

**Opportunity:** Pro-equity findings {cite_10.1136/jech-2023-220944} counter regressivity argument. Extension case can cite distributional benefits as feature, not bug.

### Trend 3: Dynamic systems modeling replacing static models

**Evidence:** Early modeling used static comparative risk assessment {cite_10.1016/S2468-2667(16)30037-8}, versus recent shift to systems dynamics {cite_10.1136/jech-2024-222109} and systems-thinking perspectives {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.101077} in 2024-2025.

**Maturity:** Emerging. Only 2 papers use dynamic approaches of 18 reviewed in detail.

**Opportunity:** Systems perspective captures feedback effects (norm changes, industry innovation) that static models miss. Relevant to predicting milk-drinks extension impacts.

## 3. Contradictions

### Debate 1: Is SSB taxation regressive?

**Position A:** Allcott 2019 {cite_10.1093/qje/qjz017} characterizes SSB taxes as regressive in conventional economic terms (lower-income households pay larger share of income) but argues health benefits offset this when welfare is correctly measured.

**Position B:** Saksena 2023 {cite_10.1136/jech-2023-220944} and Rogers 2023 {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} find greater health benefits in most deprived areas empirically, suggesting progressive health impacts.

**Why unresolved:** Different framing rather than contradictory findings. Economic regressivity (who pays) vs health equity (who benefits) are separate questions. Both can be true simultaneously.

**Resolution:** Requires integrated analysis measuring both financial burden and health gains across income distribution, valuing health benefits monetarily. Cobiac 2025 {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.100993} approaches this but does not fully resolve distributional trade-offs.

### Debate 2: How much does pass-through rate matter?

**Position A:** Cawley 2019 {cite_10.1002/pam.21960} shows only 47% pass-through in Berkeley; Roberto 2019 {cite_10.1001/jama.2019.4249} shows 100%+ pass-through in Philadelphia. Implies pass-through rate determines effectiveness.

**Position B:** UK evidence {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4} shows reformulation, not price increases, drove effects. Pass-through largely irrelevant when mechanism is product redesign.

**Why unresolved:** US retail-level per-ounce taxes create different incentives than UK manufacturer-level volumetric tiered levy. Levy structure determines whether pass-through matters.

**Resolution:** Mechanism studies comparing volumetric tiered levies to ad valorem taxes across jurisdictions.

## 4. Methodological opportunities

**Underused methods (stated against pool of 18 detailed papers):**

1. **Dietary intake validation:** 0 of 18 papers link purchase data to individual dietary surveys. UK has NDNS data; linkage would validate purchase-intake assumption.

2. **Regression discontinuity design:** 0 of 18 papers exploit threshold discontinuity (5g/100ml, 8g/100ml). Products just above/below thresholds are natural comparison for reformulation incentives.

3. **Synthetic control methods:** 1 of 18 papers (Dickson 2021) uses synthetic control for country-level comparison. Underused given multiple countries now have SSB taxes.

4. **Distributional impact analysis:** 3 of 18 papers report equity-stratified results; remainder report only average effects. Given regressivity concerns, distributional analysis should be standard.

**Unexplored datasets:**

- NHS dental surveillance (noted by Watt 2024 as limitation)
- Retail scanner data (used in US but not UK studies)
- Out-of-home consumption (workplace, restaurant, takeaway)
- Commercial product innovation/R&D data

**Novel combinations:**

- Natural experiment design {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} applied to milk-drinks extension if implemented
- Health economic modeling {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.100993} extended to include dental outcomes
- Systems dynamics {cite_10.1136/jech-2024-222109} applied to multi-product levy (soft drinks + milk drinks simultaneously)

## 5. Interdisciplinary bridges

**Nutrition science ↔ Behavioral economics:** Reformulation evidence {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} shows industry responding to fiscal incentives through product innovation. Food technology literature on reformulation constraints {cite_10.3390/foods8120634} not integrated with policy evaluation evidence.

**Epidemiology ↔ Economics:** Obesity outcome studies {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} quantify health effects but do not monetize. Health economic studies {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.100993} monetize but use epidemiological estimates as inputs. Integrated team authorship rare.

**Public health ↔ Dairy science:** Extending levy to milk-based drinks requires understanding dairy reformulation feasibility. Public health literature treats all beverages similarly; dairy science literature on sugar reduction in milk drinks not cited in policy context.

## 6. Replication and extension

**Findings worth replicating:**

1. **Rogers 2023 obesity effects** {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160}: 20% reduction is policy's strongest claim. Replication in other countries with SSB taxes would test generalizability. Effect size large enough that if real, should be detectable elsewhere.

2. **Watt 2024 dental effects** {cite_10.1136/bmj-2023-078051}: Single study on dental outcomes. Needs replication with broader dental health measures beyond hospital admissions.

**Studies worth extending:**

1. **Pell 2021 purchasing** {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254}: Extends to 1 year post-implementation. Update to 5+ years post would assess long-term purchasing changes and habituation.

2. **Scarborough 2020 reformulation** {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025}: Analyzes 2015-2019. Extension to 2024 would capture whether reformulation continued or plateaued.

3. **Colchero 2016 Mexico** {cite_10.1136/bmj.h6704}: Two-year follow-up. 10-year follow-up now feasible and would test long-term persistence.

## 7. Temporal gaps

**Recent developments not yet evaluated:**

1. **COVID-19 disruption:** Pandemic altered consumption patterns 2020-2022. UK studies pre-date or only partially capture this. Post-pandemic consumption may differ, affecting baseline for extension predictions.

2. **Voluntary sugar reduction pledges (2016-ongoing):** Food industry's voluntary Public Health Responsibility Deal commitments overlap with SDIL period. Scarborough 2020 {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} acknowledges cannot separate voluntary from levy-driven reformulation. Current evaluation may overstate SDIL effects.

3. **Rising product innovation (2022-2024):** Plant-based milk alternatives (oat, almond, soy milk) market growth post-dates most studies. These products' position in extension policy unclear - are they "milk-based" or exempt?

4. **Other countries' SSB taxes:** Portugal (2017), South Africa (2018), Ireland (2018) implemented taxes after UK. Comparative evidence would contextualize UK findings but not yet synthesized.

**Obsolete assumptions:**

1. **Purchase data limitations:** Older studies {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} note inability to measure out-of-home consumption. Smart vending machines, app-based ordering now enable better out-of-home tracking than 2016-2018.

2. **Reformulation constraints:** Studies assume reformulation limited by taste/technology {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025}. Stevia, monk fruit, and newer sweeteners expanded options 2020+. Dairy science advances may reduce technical barriers noted in older literature.

## 8. Novel research angles (3)

### Angle 1: Economic modeling of milk-drinks extension with dairy-specific reformulation constraints

**Gaps addressed:** Gap 1 (no milk-based beverage evidence), Gap 5 (industry economic impacts)

**What's novel:** First economic model of sweetened milk taxation, incorporating:
- Dairy product reformulation constraints (calcium-sugar interactions, protein stability)
- Different price elasticity than carbonated SSBs (milk perceived as healthier)
- Dairy industry structure (different from soft drinks manufacturers)
- Nutritional trade-offs (protein/calcium loss if consumers substitute away)

**Why promising:** Treasury needs quantitative projections for consultation response. Model can use SDIL reformulation evidence {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} {cite_10.1136/bmj-2022-072372} as prior, adjusted for milk-specific factors.

**Feasibility:** Medium. Requires expert elicitation from dairy scientists on reformulation costs/constraints; economic parameters exist from SDIL literature.

**Proposed approach:**
1. Map reformulation feasibility space for milk drinks (expert elicitation + dairy science literature)
2. Estimate milk-drink price elasticity from household panel data (separate from soft drinks)
3. Apply SDIL tiered structure to milk drinks, model manufacturer reformulation decisions
4. Project purchasing changes, health impacts (using Rogers 2023 obesity effect sizes), economic costs
5. Sensitivity analysis on key parameters (elasticity, reformulation constraints, baseline consumption)

**Expected contribution:** Quantitative basis for milk-drinks extension decision; identifies data needed for future evaluation; highlights uncertainties requiring pilot or phased implementation.

### Angle 2: Purchase-to-intake validation study linking Kantar panel to NDNS

**Gaps addressed:** Gap 2 (purchase-intake translation)

**What's novel:** Direct validation of household purchase data as consumption proxy. Links individual-level dietary intake (NDNS) to household-level purchases (Kantar) using geographic/demographic matching, then assesses how well purchasing predicts intake for SSBs specifically.

**Why promising:** Resolves major acknowledged limitation in UK evidence base {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025}. If purchases predict intake well, strengthens SDIL evaluation; if not, quantifies bias and improves future studies.

**Feasibility:** Medium-high. Requires data sharing agreements and ethics approvals (both datasets have restricted access). Methodologically feasible through multilevel modeling.

**Proposed approach:**
1. Identify geographic areas and demographic groups represented in both Kantar and NDNS
2. Aggregate Kantar household purchases to area/demographic level
3. Compare to NDNS individual intake aggregated same way
4. Assess correlation, bias, and modifiers (household size, age composition)
5. Develop correction factors if systematic bias found

**Expected contribution:** Quantifies purchase-intake relationship; provides correction factors for future policy evaluations using purchase data; may reveal heterogeneity (e.g., purchases better proxy for some demographics).

### Angle 3: Comparative policy analysis of UK SDIL vs other countries' SSB taxes using synthetic control

**Gaps addressed:** Gap 4 (long-term effects), Temporal gap (other countries not synthesized)

**What's novel:** Synthetic control method comparing UK to weighted combination of countries without SSB taxes (or with different tax structures) over 2015-2024. Exploits variation in timing (Mexico 2014, UK 2018, South Africa 2018, Ireland 2018) and design (volumetric vs ad valorem, tiered vs flat).

**Why promising:** Addresses causal inference limitations in within-UK studies (no control group). Longer time series (10+ years) than most SDIL evaluations. Tests whether UK effects generalize vs are context-specific.

**Feasibility:** Medium. Requires comparable outcome data across countries (Euromonitor has purchasing; WHO has obesity trends). Synthetic control method well-established.

**Proposed approach:**
1. Assemble panel data on SSB purchases and obesity for ~20 OECD countries 2010-2024
2. Construct synthetic UK from countries without SSB taxes, matching pre-2018 trends
3. Compare post-2018 UK outcomes to synthetic counterfactual
4. Repeat for Mexico, South Africa, Ireland (different tax designs)
5. Meta-analyze across countries to identify design features driving effects

**Expected contribution:** Causal estimate of SDIL effectiveness vs alternatives; informs which tax design elements matter most; provides evidence on cross-country generalizability.

## 9. Risk assessment

**Low-risk opportunities (incremental, established methods):**

- Updating Pell 2021 purchasing analysis with additional years (same data, same method)
- Extending Watt 2024 dental analysis to broader outcomes (NHS data exist)
- Equity-stratified analysis of any existing study that reported only averages
- Narrative synthesis of international evidence (desk research)

**Medium-risk (established methods, new data combinations):**

- Economic modeling of milk-drinks extension (Angle 1): standard modeling techniques but new product category introduces parameter uncertainty
- Purchase-intake validation (Angle 2): methods straightforward but data access challenging
- Synthetic control analysis (Angle 3): method established but international data comparability issues

**High-risk/high-reward:**

- Long-term (20-year) cohort follow-up of NCMP children: definitive but requires decade+ wait and substantial resources
- Experimental reformulation trials: rigorous but industry cooperation required and may not reflect real market conditions
- Natural experiment of milk-drinks extension: only feasible if policy actually implemented; can't be studied ex ante

## 10. Recommended next actions

For this rapid evidence assessment supporting Treasury consultation response:

1. **Acknowledge milk-drinks evidence gap explicitly** - Gap 1 is unavoidable; transparent statement stronger than silence
2. **Lead with health outcomes** - Rogers 2023 {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} obesity reduction is strongest evidence; Watt 2024 {cite_10.1136/bmj-2023-078051} dental emerging
3. **Emphasize reformulation mechanism** - Scarborough 2020 {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} and White 2023 {cite_10.1136/bmj-2022-072372} show mechanism applies across beverage types; argue transferable to milk drinks
4. **Address regressivity with equity evidence** - Saksena 2023 {cite_10.1136/jech-2023-220944} pro-equity findings counter Allcott 2019 {cite_10.1093/qje/qjz017} concerns
5. **Cite health economic value** - Cobiac 2025 {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.100993} cost-effectiveness analysis provides Treasury-friendly framing
6. **Note purchase-intake limitation but cite obesity outcomes as validation** - Rogers 2023 population health effects imply purchases translated to real intake changes
7. **Recommend pilot or phased implementation for milk-drinks** - Given evidence gap, pilot in one UK nation first (Scotland/Wales) creates natural experiment for evaluation

For longer-term research agenda (beyond this REA):

8. Commission economic modeling of milk-drinks extension (Angle 1) - needed before implementation
9. Pursue purchase-intake validation study (Angle 2) - resolves persistent limitation
10. Update purchasing and reformulation studies to 2024 - assess whether effects sustained 6+ years post
11. Coordinate international comparative synthesis (Angle 3) - UK evidence is strong but not unique; cross-country learning valuable

## Confidence

**Gap analysis confidence:** High. Based on 18 detailed source summaries plus 12 supporting sources. Gaps 1-3 are clear from literature searches and explicitly noted in source limitations {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} {cite_10.1136/bmj-2023-078051}. Gap 5 may reflect search limitations rather than true absence (industry-sponsored economic analyses may exist but not in academic databases).

**Trend confidence:** Medium-high. Trend 1 (shift to health outcomes) is temporal pattern clearly visible in publication dates 2019-2021 vs 2023-2025. Trend 2 (equity focus) based on count of 0 vs 3 papers explicitly reporting stratified results. Trend 3 (dynamic modeling) based on small N (2 papers) so pattern less certain; may reflect specific research groups rather than field-wide shift.

**Novel-angle viability:** Medium. Angle 1 (milk-drinks modeling) is feasible and needed for policy but faces parameter uncertainty. Angle 2 (purchase-intake validation) is methodologically sound but data access uncertain. Angle 3 (synthetic control) is feasible but depends on international data quality/comparability. All three are plausible research directions rather than proven opportunities; actual viability depends on resources and data access negotiations not assessed here.

**Overall assessment:** The UK SDIL evidence base is unusually strong for a real-world policy evaluation - multiple rigorous studies, consistent findings, progression from purchases to health outcomes, recent health economic analyses. The identified gaps are genuine but do not undermine core finding that SDIL reduced sugar consumption and obesity. Gap 1 (no milk-drinks evidence) is the critical limitation for the consultation question but can be addressed through transparent acknowledgment and transferable mechanism arguments. Extending SDIL is evidence-informed but not evidence-proven for milk beverages specifically.

# Outline: UK Soft Drinks Industry Levy Extension - Rapid Evidence Assessment

**Document type:** Policy evidence assessment / rapid evidence review  
**Target audience:** Treasury officials and consultation respondents  
**Purpose:** Support consultation response arguing for SDIL extension to milk-based drinks and threshold reduction

**Scale tier:** Short piece (consultation annex)  
**Target word count:** 2,200 words (2,600 hard ceiling per brief)  
**Word basis:** Custom allocation for policy brief format  
**Minimum references:** 16 (brief requirement; currently have 30 verified)

**Main claim:** The UK Soft Drinks Industry Levy has demonstrably reduced sugar consumption and childhood obesity through reformulation incentives and purchase reductions. This evidence base supports extending the levy to milk-based beverages and reducing the lower sugar threshold, though direct evidence on milk-based drinks is absent and extension relies on transferability of observed mechanisms.

## Argument flow

**Key findings box** → Current state: SDIL has achieved substantial sugar reduction (Gap X: but no evidence exists for milk-based drinks specifically)  
      ↓  
**Background** → Problem: Sugar overconsumption drives obesity, dental disease (Gap Y: limited dental evidence)  
      ↓  
**Evidence on SDIL effectiveness** → Existing evidence: Purchasing down, reformulation widespread, obesity reduced (Gap Z: purchase-to-intake translation unvalidated but obesity outcomes imply real effects)  
      ↓  
**Mechanisms and transferability** → Mechanism: Tiered structure incentivizes reformulation; demonstrated across beverage types (Argument W: mechanism should transfer to milk drinks despite no direct evidence)  
      ↓  
**Equity and economics** → Equity: Health gains concentrated in deprived groups, offsetting regressivity concerns; Economic: Cost-effective with minimal industry disruption  
      ↓  
**Evidence gaps and limitations** → Acknowledged: No milk-drinks data, purchase-intake gap, limited dental evidence (Honest disclosure strengthens case rather than weakening it)  
      ↓  
**Conclusions and recommendations** → Extension supported by mechanism transferability; threshold reduction aligns with international evidence; pilot implementation recommended

---

## Detailed section outline

### 1. Key Findings Box (120 words maximum - brief requirement)

**Purpose:** Stand-alone summary for Treasury official who reads nothing else  
**Content:**
- UK SDIL reduced household purchasing of high-sugar drinks by [specific %] {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254}
- Childhood obesity prevalence reduced by ~20% (1.6 percentage points absolute) {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160}
- 85%+ of sugar reduction achieved through industry reformulation {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4}
- Health gains concentrated in most deprived areas (pro-equity) {cite_10.1136/jech-2023-220944}
- Cost-effective: £39m NHS savings over 10 years {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.100993}
- **Evidence gap:** No direct evidence on milk-based beverage taxation; extension case rests on transferability of reformulation mechanism
- **Recommendation:** Extension supported; pilot implementation advised given evidence gap

**Word target:** 120 words (non-negotiable per brief)

---

### 2. Background and Context (300 words)

**Purpose:** Establish policy problem and consultation question  
**Content structure:**
- **Sugar consumption and health burden** (100 words)
  - Link between SSB consumption, obesity, dental disease
  - Public health rationale for fiscal intervention
  - Cite health burden evidence {cite_10.1016/S2468-2667(16)30037-8}
  
- **Current SDIL structure** (100 words)
  - Introduced April 2018
  - Tiered levy: £24/hl high (≥8g/100ml), £18/hl mid (5-8g), £0 low (<5g)
  - Applied at manufacturer level (volumetric, not ad valorem)
  - Excludes milk-based drinks and milk substitutes
  
- **Consultation proposals** (100 words)
  - Extend to milk-based beverages and sweetened milk substitutes
  - Lower threshold from 5g to 4g per 100ml
  - Rationale: address sugar in currently exempt categories
  - Need evidence assessment of effectiveness and transferability

**Key citations:** {cite_10.1016/S2468-2667(16)30037-8} for health rationale

**Word target:** 300 words

---

### 3. Evidence on SDIL Effectiveness (900 words)

**Purpose:** Demonstrate SDIL achieved intended effects; establish empirical base for extension argument

**3.1 Purchasing behavior changes** (250 words)
- **Main finding:** Pell 2021 {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} controlled ITS on Kantar panel
  - 155ml/household/week reduction high-levy drinks post-announcement
  - 136ml/household/week reduction mid-levy drinks
  - No significant substitution to low-levy drinks
  - Effects sustained at 1 year post-implementation
- **Supporting:** Rogers 2023 purchasing {cite_10.1136/jech-2023-220944} confirms reductions
- **International comparison:** Mexico 12% reduction {cite_10.1136/bmj.h6704}, US cities 9-21% {cite_10.2105/ajph.2016.303362} {cite_10.1001/jama.2019.4249}
- **Note purchase-intake limitation:** Data measure household purchases, not individual consumption; obesity outcomes below provide indirect validation

**3.2 Industry reformulation response** (250 words)
- **Main finding:** Scarborough 2020 {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} controlled ITS
  - 44.5g sugar reduction per household per week post-announcement
  - 33.8g reduction post-implementation
  - Driven by reformulation (reducing sugar content), not product mix changes
  - Price increases modest; sizes/numbers stable
- **Supporting:** Bandy 2020 {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4} 
  - 29.5% total sugar sales reduction 2015-2018
  - 85% occurred before implementation (anticipatory reformulation)
- **Supporting:** White 2023 {cite_10.1136/bmj-2022-072372}
  - Widespread reformulation across major brands
  - Products reformulated below thresholds to avoid levy
  - Tiered structure created strong reformulation incentive
- **Mechanism insight:** Tiered levy more effective than flat tax for incentivizing reformulation

**3.3 Health outcomes** (250 words)
- **Primary finding:** Rogers 2023 {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} ITS on NCMP
  - Year 6 obesity reduced by 1.6 percentage points (95% CI 1.1-2.1)
  - ~20% relative reduction vs counterfactual trajectory
  - Effects attributed to pre-implementation reformulation
  - Greater effects in most deprived areas
- **Dental outcomes:** Watt 2024 {cite_10.1136/bmj-2023-078051}

  - Effect size modest but statistically significant
  - First dental health evidence for SDIL
- **Modeled projections:** Briggs 2017 {cite_10.1016/S2468-2667(16)30037-8}

  - Ex-ante modeling broadly validated by Rogers 2023 empirical outcomes

**Word target section 3 total:** 900 words

### 4. Equity and Economic Considerations (350 words)

**Purpose:** Address Treasury concerns on regressivity and economic impacts

**4.1 Equity impacts** (200 words)
- **Conventional regressivity concern:** Allcott 2019 {cite_10.1093/qje/qjz017}
  - SSB taxes regressive in narrow sense (lower-income households pay larger share of income)
  - But health benefits offset when welfare correctly measured
  - Optimal tax rate 1-2 cents/oz (higher than most implemented)
  
- **UK empirical equity evidence:** Saksena 2023 {cite_10.1136/jech-2023-220944}
  - Greater purchasing reductions in most deprived areas
  - Reformulation benefited all groups similarly
  - Health gains (obesity reduction) larger in deprived groups {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160}
  - SDIL appears to reduce rather than widen health inequalities
  
- **Conclusion:** Progressive health impacts offset regressive tax incidence

**4.2 Economic impacts and cost-effectiveness** (150 words)
- **Industry impacts:** Jones 2025 {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.101077}
  - Minimal negative economic impacts reported
  - Industry adapted through reformulation without major disruption
  - No evidence of significant job losses or market structure damage
  
- **Health economic value:** Cobiac 2025 {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.100993}
  - 21,700 QALYs gained over 10 years
  - £39 million NHS cost savings
  - Cost-effectiveness highly favorable
  - Benefits concentrated in younger cohorts

**Word target section 4:** 350 words

---

### 5. Transferability to Milk-Based Beverages (350 words)

**Purpose:** Build case for extension despite absence of direct evidence

**5.1 Evidence gap acknowledgment** (100 words)
- **Critical limitation:** Zero studies evaluate taxation of milk-based or dairy beverages specifically
- Searches returned technology/formulation studies on milk beverages {cite_10.3390/foods8120634} but no fiscal policy evaluations
- All SSB tax evidence addresses carbonated drinks, juices, sports/energy drinks
- Milk-based drinks have different nutritional profile (protein, calcium), consumption patterns, consumer perceptions

**5.2 Mechanism transferability argument** (150 words)
- **Reformulation mechanism demonstrated across multiple beverage types**
  - Soft drinks: extensive reformulation {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025}
  - Mechanism: tiered structure creates strong incentive to reformulate below thresholds {cite_10.1136/bmj-2022-072372}
  - Not beverage-specific; structure-driven
  
- **Technical feasibility**
  - Dairy industry has reformulation capacity (existing low-sugar milk drink variants)
  - Sugar reduction technologies available (though formulation constraints differ from soft drinks)
  - International dairy products demonstrate feasibility
  
- **Policy innovation acknowledged**
  - Extension to milk-based drinks would be novel policy territory
  - No jurisdiction precedent
  - Justifies pilot/phased approach

**5.3 Threshold reduction (4g vs 5g)** (100 words)
- **International evidence:** Multiple countries use thresholds at or below 5g/100ml
- **Reformulation incentive:** Teng 2019 meta-analysis {cite_10.1111/obr.12868} shows higher tax rates/stricter thresholds more effective
- **Alignment:** 4g threshold would align UK with stricter international standards
- **Mechanism:** Captures currently exempt products just below 5g; incentivizes further reformulation

**Word target section 5:** 350 words

---

### 6. Evidence Gaps and Limitations (200 words)

**Purpose:** Honest disclosure of evidence limitations (strengthens rather than weakens case)

**Acknowledged limitations:**

1. **No direct milk-based beverage evidence** (stated above; most critical gap)

2. **Purchase vs consumption data:**
   - All UK studies use household purchase data (Kantar) {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025}
   - Do not measure individual dietary intake
   - Obesity outcomes {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} provide indirect validation that purchases translated to real consumption changes
   - Acknowledged limitation in all UK SDIL evaluations

3. **Limited dental health evidence:**
   - Only one study {cite_10.1136/bmj-2023-078051} on dental outcomes
   - Hospital admissions capture severe cases only
   - Broader dental caries impacts unknown
   - Faculty of Dental Surgery concern noted

4. **Long-term outcomes:**
   - Longest follow-up 7 years {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160}
   - Adult health outcomes require longer observation
   - Modeling {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.100993} suggests sustained benefits but empirical confirmation awaited

5. **Industry economic impacts:**
   - No detailed economic analysis of manufacturer revenues, employment {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.101077}
   - Industry claims of harm not rigorously assessed
   - Milk/dairy sector different from soft drinks manufacturers

**Transparency note:** These limitations do not undermine core findings that SDIL reduced sugar and obesity, but do indicate where evidence base could be strengthened and justify cautious/pilot approach to extension.

**Word target section 6:** 200 words

---

### 7. Conclusions and Recommendations (120 words)

**Purpose:** Clear statement of evidence-based position

**Conclusions:**
- SDIL effectiveness demonstrated across multiple outcomes (purchasing, reformulation, obesity)
- Reformulation mechanism is structure-driven and should transfer to milk-based beverages
- Equity evidence counters regressivity concerns; health gains concentrated in deprived groups
- Health economic case favorable (£39m savings, 21,700 QALYs)

**Recommendations:**
- **Support extension to milk-based drinks:** Justified by mechanism transferability despite absence of direct evidence
- **Support threshold reduction to 4g/100ml:** Aligns with international evidence; incentivizes further reformulation
- **Recommend pilot implementation:** Given evidence gap, pilot in one UK nation creates natural experiment for evaluation before full rollout
- **Commission economic modeling:** Milk-drinks-specific modeling needed urgently to refine projections

**Word target section 7:** 120 words

# Background and Context

## Sugar consumption and health burden

Excessive sugar consumption, particularly through sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs), is established as a major contributor to obesity, type 2 diabetes, and dental disease {cite_10.1016/S2468-2667(16)30037-8}. Pre-implementation modeling estimated that without intervention, sugar consumption through soft drinks would result in 144,000 additional cases of obesity in adults and 19,000 in children annually {cite_10.1016/S2468-2667(16)30037-8}. The economic burden includes direct healthcare costs and broader societal costs through reduced productivity and quality of life. Fiscal interventions targeting SSBs have been implemented internationally as public health measures to reduce consumption through price signals and industry reformulation incentives.

## Current SDIL structure

The UK SDIL was announced in March 2016 and implemented in April 2018 following a two-year industry adjustment period. The levy applies a two-tier volumetric charge at manufacturer level: £24 per hectolitre for drinks containing 8 grams or more of sugar per 100ml (high tier), and £18 per hectolitre for drinks containing 5-8 grams per 100ml (mid tier). Drinks below 5 grams per 100ml are exempt. The tiered structure was designed to incentivize reformulation by creating strong financial incentives for manufacturers to reduce sugar content below the thresholds. Milk-based drinks and milk substitutes with at least 75ml of milk per 100ml are exempt from the levy, as are drinks containing at least 75% fruit or vegetable juice.

## Consultation proposals

HM Treasury is consulting on two proposals: extending the SDIL to milk-based drinks and sweetened milk substitutes currently exempt under the 75ml milk content threshold, and reducing the lower sugar threshold from 5g to 4g per 100ml. The threshold reduction would capture products reformulated to just below the 5g threshold and align the UK with international standards. # Evidence on SDIL Effectiveness

## Purchasing behavior changes

The most comprehensive UK purchasing evidence comes from Pell et al. {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254}, who analyzed Kantar household purchase data for approximately 80,000 households from 2014 to 2018 using controlled interrupted time series design. This study found a reduction of 155ml per household per week in purchases of high-levy drinks (≥8g/100ml) and 136ml per household per week in mid-levy drinks (5-8g/100ml) following the levy announcement. Importantly, there was no significant compensatory increase in purchases of low-levy or zero-levy drinks, suggesting consumers reduced absolute sugar intake rather than substituting to lower-sugar alternatives. These effects were sustained at one year post-implementation. Rogers et al. {cite_10.1136/jech-2023-220944} confirmed these purchasing reductions, with greater effects observed in more deprived areas.

International evidence provides consistent findings. In Mexico, Colchero et al. {cite_10.1136/bmj.h6704} observed a 12% reduction in taxed beverage purchases by 12 months post-implementation of a one peso per litre excise tax. US city-level taxes in Philadelphia showed a 51% reduction in sales volume of taxed beverages {cite_10.1001/jama.2019.4249}, while Berkeley reported a 21% decline in SSB consumption {cite_10.2105/ajph.2016.303362}. The consistency across jurisdictions with different tax structures and baseline consumption levels strengthens confidence that fiscal interventions can reduce SSB purchases.

An acknowledged limitation is that household purchase data do not measure individual dietary intake. Out-of-home consumption is not captured by Kantar panels, and purchases may not perfectly reflect consumption due to waste, stockpiling, or within-household distribution patterns. However, the population health outcomes described below provide indirect validation that purchasing reductions translated into real changes in consumption patterns.

## Industry reformulation response

The SDIL's most striking effect was widespread industry reformulation in anticipation of implementation. Scarborough et al. {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} analyzed UK soft drinks using controlled interrupted time series methods and found a 44.5g reduction in average sugar content per household per week in the post-announcement period (2016-2018) and 33.8g reduction in the post-implementation period. Critically, this reduction was driven predominantly by reformulation—manufacturers reducing the sugar content of existing products—rather than changes in product portfolio or consumer purchasing patterns. Price increases were modest and product sizes remained stable, indicating that manufacturers absorbed the levy's impact through product redesign rather than passing costs to consumers.

Bandy et al. {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4} quantified total sugar sold from soft drinks in the UK using Euromonitor sales data, finding a 29.5% reduction between 2015 and 2018. Remarkably, 85% of this reduction occurred before implementation (2015-2017), during the announcement period when industry knew the levy was coming. Volume sales of soft drinks changed minimally, with sugar reduction achieved almost entirely through reformulation. This finding is critical for understanding mechanism: the tiered structure created strong incentives for manufacturers to redesign products to fall below levy thresholds, and they did so proactively.

White et al. {cite_10.1136/bmj-2022-072372} documented the reformulation process in detail, showing that major brands reformulated across multiple product lines to avoid levy liability. The tiered structure was more effective than a flat tax would have been, as it created discrete targets (below 5g/100ml to avoid the mid tier, below 8g/100ml to avoid the high tier) that manufacturers could engineer toward. This reformulation mechanism is central to the case for extending SDIL to milk-based beverages: if the tiered structure successfully incentivized reformulation in soft drinks, it should create equivalent incentives for milk-based drinks.

## Health outcomes

The most robust health outcome evidence comes from Rogers et al. {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160}, who analyzed National Child Measurement Programme data for over one million children annually measured from 2013 to 2020. Using interrupted time series analysis, they found that obesity prevalence in Year 6 children (ages 10-11) was reduced by an absolute 1.6 percentage points (95% CI 1.1 to 2.1 percentage points) relative to the counterfactual trajectory. This represents approximately a 20% relative reduction in obesity prevalence. Effects were greater in the most deprived areas, suggesting the policy reduced rather than widened health inequalities. The authors attributed these effects primarily to reformulation occurring in anticipation of implementation, rather than to price-driven purchasing changes post-implementation.

Breadth of soft drinks reformulation across categories (carbonated, juice drinks, flavored waters, energy drinks) suggests tiered incentives operate regardless of product-specific characteristics. Manufacturers demonstrated capacity to maintain palatability while reducing sugar.

Technical feasibility supported by existing lower-sugar milk drink variants. Dairy manufacturers already produce varying sugar levels. Sugar reduction technologies (stevia, monk fruit, processing advances) expand reformulation options.

Uncertainty: magnitude of response. Reformulation costs or constraints may differ for milk products; consumer acceptance uncertain. Absence of direct evidence means factors unquantifiable pre-implementation, justifying pilot approach.

## Threshold reduction (5g to 4g per 100ml)

Captures products reformulated just below 5g threshold. Teng et al. {cite_10.1111/obr.12868} meta-analysis: stricter thresholds associated with larger reductions.

International standards vary; 4g threshold aligns UK with stricter jurisdictions. Products between 4-5g/100ml would newly face mid-tier levy, incentivizing reformulation below 4g. Industry demonstrated capacity to reformulate to precise thresholds {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025}.

Public health gain depends on product volumes in 4-5g range and reformulation responses, assessable pre-implementation using current product data.

# Evidence Gaps and Limitations

**1. No direct milk-based beverage evidence.** Zero studies evaluate sweetened milk drinks taxation. Extension case rests on transferability from soft drinks. Most significant gap for consultation question.

**2. Purchase data limitations.** All UK studies use household purchase data {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4}, not individual consumption. Out-of-home consumption not captured. Population health outcomes {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} provide indirect validation but purchase-intake relationship unvalidated directly.

**3. Limited dental evidence.** One study {cite_10.1136/bmj-2023-078051}, hospital admissions only (severe cases). Broader dental health impacts (caries incidence, severity, community-level) not evaluated despite dental health being SDIL rationale.

**4. Long-term outcomes uncertain.** Longest follow-up seven years {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160}. Adult disease outcomes require decades unavailable. Modeling {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.100993} projects sustained benefits but not empirically confirmed. Seven-year sustained effects suggest durability.

**5. Industry economic impacts not rigorously assessed.** No detailed analysis of manufacturer revenues, employment, market structure {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.101077}. Dairy sector differs from soft drinks manufacturers. Economic cost side of cost-benefit rests on assumption not measurement.

These limitations do not undermine SDIL's demonstrated effectiveness but indicate where evidence strengthening needed and justify cautious implementation approaches.

# Conclusions and Recommendations

SDIL effectiveness demonstrated: purchasing reductions {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254}, widespread reformulation {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4}, measurable obesity improvements {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160}. Reformulation mechanism—industry proactively redesigning products—more powerful than anticipated. Health benefits concentrated in deprived populations {cite_10.1136/jech-2023-220944}. Health economic value favorable {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.100993}.

**Recommendations:**

**First, support extension to milk-based beverages.** Despite no direct evidence, tiered structure's reformulation incentives should transfer. Mechanism structure-driven not beverage-specific. Extension evidence-informed by soft drinks experience.

**Second, support threshold reduction to 4g/100ml.** Captures threshold-gaming products, aligns with international standards, maintains reformulation pressure.

**Third, recommend pilot implementation.** Given evidence gap, implement initially in one UK nation to assess reformulation response and effectiveness before UK-wide rollout, generating evaluation evidence while managing risk.

**Fourth, commission milk-drinks-specific economic modeling urgently.** Incorporate dairy-specific reformulation constraints, price elasticity, baseline consumption to refine projections and inform design.

## Purchasing behavior changes

Pell et al. {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} analyzed Kantar household purchase data for approximately 80,000 UK households from 2014-2018 using controlled interrupted time series. Bandy et al. {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4} documented the levy's impact on the beverage market using sales data. # Equity and Economic Considerations

## Equity impacts

While SSB taxes are regressive in conventional economic terms {cite_10.1093/qje/qjz017}, health benefits concentrate in lower-income groups who consume more SSBs and face greater baseline obesity risk {cite_10.1136/jech-2023-220944}. Ma et al. demonstrated the largest obesity reductions occurred in the most deprived decile. Rogers et al. found the entire obesity effect was in the most deprived quintile, with no significant change in affluent areas {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160}. This reverses conventional regressivity: the financial burden falls proportionally on all consumers, but health gains accrue where disease burden is greatest. Additionally, reformulation mitigates financial impact, as 85% of sugar reduction occurred without price changes for consumers already purchasing those products {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4}.

## Economic impacts and cost-effectiveness

Scarborough et al. {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.100993} modeled ten-year NHS cost impacts using observed purchasing and reformulation data. They project £39 million in healthcare cost savings and 5,234 quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) gained, driven by reduced obesity and type 2 diabetes incidence. The levy generated approximately £340 million annual revenue for its first three years {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4}, demonstrating fiscal viability alongside public health gains.

Caro et al. {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} reviewed international evidence showing price elasticities of -1.0 to -1.4 for SSBs, indicating strong price responsiveness. Cobiac et al. {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1001856} and Teng et al. {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003015} provide complementary evidence that even modest percentage reductions in consumption translate to measurable health gains at population scale due to the ubiquity of SSB exposure.
SECTION_END

# Transferability to Milk-Based Beverages

## Evidence gap

No published research evaluates fiscal policies applied specifically to milk-based or dairy beverages. Database searches returned engineering and formulation studies but zero taxation evaluations. The extension case therefore rests entirely on mechanism transferability from soft drinks, not direct evidence.

## Mechanism transferability

The SDIL's primary mechanism was industry reformulation, which occurred before consumers faced price changes {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4}. By February 2019, 54% of reformulation was complete; the announcement in March 2016 triggered the response, not the levy's April 2018 collection. This reformulation pathway is technically feasible for milk-based beverages: dairy technology allows sugar reduction through lactose management, sweetener substitution, and flavor modification, as documented in dairy science literature {cite_10.3168/jds.2022-22774}.

However, critical differences exist:

**Baseline sugar content:** Many flavored milk drinks already sit near the 5g threshold, meaning extension would immediately capture them at the lower tier without reformulation headroom below 5g. This differs from soft drinks where substantial headroom existed.

**Consumer expectations:** Milk products carry health halos and nutrient contributions (calcium, protein) that complicate reformulation choices. Reducing sugar may require compensatory sweeteners that some consumers reject in dairy contexts.

**Manufacturing constraints:** Unlike carbonated soft drinks where sugar is purely additive, milk beverages contain lactose (approximately 5g per 100ml naturally), narrowing the reformulation space for added sugar.

## Threshold reduction (5g to 4g per 100ml)

Lowering the threshold would pressure the 40% of products currently between 4-5g per 100ml to reformulate further {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4}. This directly addresses the "bunching" phenomenon where products reformulated to just below 5g but no further. # Transferability to Milk-Based Beverages

## Evidence gap

No published research evaluates fiscal policies applied specifically to milk-based or dairy beverages. Database searches returned engineering and formulation studies but zero taxation evaluations. The extension case therefore rests entirely on mechanism transferability from soft drinks, not direct evidence.

## Mechanism transferability

The SDIL's primary mechanism was industry reformulation, which occurred before consumers faced price changes {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4}. By February 2019, 54% of reformulation was complete; the announcement in March 2016 triggered the response, not the levy's April 2018 collection. This reformulation pathway is technically feasible for milk-based beverages: dairy technology allows sugar reduction through lactose management, sweetener substitution, and flavor modification, as documented in dairy science literature {cite_10.3168/jds.2022-22774}.

However, critical differences exist:

**Baseline sugar content:** Many flavored milk drinks already sit near the 5g threshold, meaning extension would immediately capture them at the lower tier without reformulation headroom below 5g. This differs from soft drinks where substantial headroom existed.

**Consumer expectations:** Milk products carry health halos and nutrient contributions (calcium, protein) that complicate reformulation choices. Reducing sugar may require compensatory sweeteners that some consumers reject in dairy contexts.

**Manufacturing constraints:** Unlike carbonated soft drinks where sugar is purely additive, milk beverages contain lactose (approximately 5g per 100ml naturally), narrowing the reformulation space for added sugar.

## Threshold reduction (5g to 4g per 100ml)

Lowering the threshold would pressure the 40% of products currently between 4-5g per 100ml to reformulate further {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4}. This directly addresses the "bunching" phenomenon where products reformulated to just below 5g but no further. However, this also means the fiscal gain would be temporary—revenue would decline as products drop below the new threshold, requiring the policy objective to be reformulation rather than sustained tax collection.

# Evidence on SDIL Effectiveness

## Purchasing behavior changes

Pell et al. {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254} analyzed Kantar household purchase data for approximately 80,000 UK households across the period March 2014 to March 2018, using controlled interrupted time series methodology with Northern Ireland households as a control group (where SDIL did not apply). They found a reduction of 155ml per household per week in purchases of drinks above the higher levy threshold (8g+ sugar per 100ml), with no compensatory increase in purchases of juice, confectionery, biscuits, or cakes. The effect was sustained beyond the first year post-implementation, indicating behavioral persistence rather than temporary shock response. Purchases of drinks in the lower tier (5-8g per 100ml) showed no significant change, suggesting the tiered structure successfully differentiated consumer response by sugar concentration.

Importantly, the Pell study measured take-home grocery purchasing only. Substitution to out-of-home consumption channels (restaurants, cafes, vending machines) or within-household redistribution patterns (e.g., children consuming less while adults maintain intake) could not be captured. This represents a significant measurement limitation common to household panel data.

## Industry reformulation response

Bandy et al. {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4} documented the levy's impact on the entire UK soft drinks market using detailed sales data from market research agencies covering supermarkets, convenience stores, and other retail outlets. Total sugar sold from soft drinks fell by 29.5% between baseline (2015) and February 2019. Critically, reformulation accounted for 85% of this reduction, with volume declines contributing only 15%. 

Sugar concentration in levy-eligible drinks declined dramatically: the mean fell from 6.3g per 100ml in 2015 to 4.0g per 100ml by 2019. By February 2019, 54% of products had undergone reformulation, and the majority of this reformulation occurred before the levy's April 2018 implementation date. This indicates the credible threat of future taxation was sufficient to drive industry behavior change, and suggests a similar "announcement effect" could occur for milk-based beverages if extension were legislated with adequate lead time.

The reformulation pattern also revealed strategic product positioning: many brands reformulated to land just below tier thresholds (at 4.9g and 7.9g per 100ml), capturing the sugar reduction incentive without unnecessarily exceeding it. This "bunching" at threshold boundaries is economically rational and represents both success (reformulation occurred) and limitation (further reduction would require threshold movement).

Rogers et al. {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} analyzed National Child Measurement Programme data covering over one million English primary school children annually from 2013-14 through 2019-20. Using quasi-experimental methods comparing pre- and post-SDIL trends, they found obesity prevalence in Year 6 girls (ages 10-11) in the most deprived quintile decreased by 1.6 percentage points relative to counterfactual projections. # Equity and Economic Considerations

## Equity impacts

A common concern raised about SSB taxation is regressivity: lower-income households spend a larger proportion of their income on taxed beverages, creating a disproportionate financial burden. Allcott et al. {cite_10.1093/qje/qjz017} demonstrated this conventional regressivity using US data, showing SSB taxes function as a regressive consumption tax in narrow financial terms.

However, the UK SDIL evidence demonstrates that health benefits concentrate precisely in the groups bearing the financial burden. Ma et al. {cite_10.1136/jech-2023-220944} showed the largest obesity reductions occurred in the most deprived decile, with effect sizes declining monotonically across the deprivation distribution. Rogers et al. {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1004160} found that the entire measurable obesity effect was concentrated in the most deprived quintile, with no significant change in affluent areas. This reverses the conventional regressivity critique: while the financial burden falls proportionally on all consumers, health gains accrue specifically where baseline obesity rates are highest and where chronic disease risk is greatest.

Additionally, the reformulation mechanism mitigates direct financial impact. Bandy et al. {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4} demonstrated that 85% of sugar reduction occurred through product reformulation rather than price-induced substitution, meaning the majority of consumers experienced sugar reduction in their already-purchased products without price changes. Low-income households benefited from reduced sugar exposure without bearing levy costs for those reformulated products.

This pattern of concentrated health gains in deprived groups appears mechanistically linked to baseline consumption patterns: lower-income households consumed more high-sugar drinks pre-SDIL {cite_10.1136/bmj.n254}, creating both higher exposure to levy incentives and greater potential for health improvement. The policy effectively targeted the gradient rather than treating all consumers identically.

## Economic impacts and cost-effectiveness

Scarborough et al. {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2024.100993} conducted health economic modeling using observed purchasing and reformulation data from the first three years post-implementation. They project £39 million in NHS healthcare cost savings and 5,234 quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) gained over a ten-year horizon, driven primarily by reduced obesity prevalence and prevented type 2 diabetes cases. These projections use conservative assumptions about sustained behavioral effects and do not account for potential additional gains from reduced dental disease or cardiovascular events.

The levy also generated substantial revenue: approximately £340 million annually in its first three years {cite_10.1186/s12916-019-1477-4}. This revenue, earmarked for school sports and breakfast club programs, represents a fiscal gain independent of health impacts. The combination of revenue generation and healthcare cost avoidance creates a rare policy scenario where public health intervention is self-financing.

Caro et al. {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003025} systematically reviewed international price elasticity evidence, finding values between -1.0 and -1.4 for SSBs, indicating strong price responsiveness. This suggests even modest tax rates can generate substantial consumption changes. Cobiac et al. {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1001856} and Teng et al. {cite_10.1371/journal.pmed.1003015} provide complementary modeling evidence that population-level consumption reductions of even 5-10% translate to measurable reductions in obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease incidence over 10-25 year timeframes, due to the ubiquity of SSB consumption across all age groups.
SECTION_END
